query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres is governed by the oxidation kinetics and thermodynamics of the alloying elements. Specifically, when X is Al or Si, their propensity to form thermodynamically stable, slow-growing, and adherent oxides (such as Al2O3 or silicate compounds) in cooperation with chromium leads to a dense, coherent oxide scale. In contrast, when X is Mn, the faster diffusion and oxidation results in less stable oxide formation that tends to be porous, prone to rapid growth, and susceptible to cracking or spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state
generation.intervention: Expose these alloys to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere above 900 °C
generation.conditions: Testing is carried out in a controlled environment with a defined oxygen partial pressure (or equivalent corrosive species) at temperatures exceeding 900 °C; variations in the X element (Al, Si, or Mn) allow for a controlled comparison against a baseline alloy composition using Mn.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructure of the surface oxide layer, including its phase composition (e.g., presence of Al2O3 or silicate compounds versus less-protective Mn-oxides) and its coherence at the metal/oxide interface, mediates the observed behavior.
generation.mechanism: The thermodynamic stability and oxidation kinetics of the added element X determine the type and quality of oxide formed. Al and Si favor the formation of slow-growing, adherent, and coherent oxide scales by stabilizing chromia and forming their own protective phases, which act as diffusion barriers to oxygen. Conversely, Mn oxidizes more rapidly, leading to a porous, non-coherent oxide which is prone to cracking or spallation due to internal stresses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Al or Si will develop a stable and coherent protective oxide layer that persists during prolonged exposure above 900 °C, while alloys with Mn will exhibit unstable oxide layers that crack or spall, resulting in higher oxidation rates.
generation.baseline: The baseline for comparison is provided by alloys with Mn as the variable element, where unstable oxide layer formation is expected due to its less favorable oxidation characteristics compared to Al or Si.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under high-temperature conditions (>900 °C) in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres, and for materials in the form of single-phase or multiphase metallic solid solutions.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in quantitatively predicting the exact growth rates and stress thresholds that differentiate stable from unstable oxide layers. The influence of the multiphase microstructure on local oxidation kinetics is also not fully resolved.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys with identical base compositions varying only in the X element (Al, Si, or Mn) and in controlled single-phase and multiphase conditions. Expose samples to a controlled oxidative/corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for predetermined durations. Characterize the oxide layers using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and measure mass gain to evaluate oxidation behavior.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and morphology (via SEM/TEM)
Phase composition of the oxide scale (via XRD)
Evidence of spalling or cracking on the surface
Mass gain as an indicator of oxidation rate
Interfacial coherence between the metal substrate and oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if alloys containing Mn display coalescence of a stable, adherent, and coherent oxide layer similar in quality to those containing Al or Si, or if the Al and Si containing alloys fail to develop the predicted protective oxide while exhibiting oxide characteristics (growth rate, cracking/spallation behavior) similar to the Mn variant.
